title: Check if Grid can be Cut into Sections
statement:
An `n x n` grid has its origin at the bottom-left corner. Each `rectangles[i] = [startX, startY, endX, endY]` is a rectangle drawn on it, with bottom-left corner `(startX, startY)` and top-right corner `(endX, endY)`. No two rectangles overlap, although they may share edges or corners.

Decide whether you can draw either two horizontal lines or two vertical lines across the grid so that:

- no line runs through the inside of a rectangle, so every rectangle lies entirely within one of the three strips the lines create (running along a rectangle's edge is fine), and
- none of those three strips is empty: each holds at least one rectangle.

Return `true` if such a pair of lines exists and `false` otherwise.
notes:
## Intuition

A horizontal line `y = c` is allowed exactly when no rectangle has `c` strictly between its `startY` and `endY`. So only each rectangle's span on one axis matters. Merge the spans that overlap (spans that merely touch stay apart, because a line may run along a shared edge): each merged **block** is a stretch no line can cross, and a line fits between any two neighbouring blocks. Two lines with a rectangle in every section therefore exist exactly when some axis has at least three blocks. A brute force would try every pair of rectangle edges as the two lines and check the sections directly.

## Approach

1. `countBlocks(from, to)` takes every rectangle's span `[rect[from], rect[to]]` on one axis: indices 0 and 2 for x, 1 and 3 for y.
2. Sort the spans by their start.
3. Scan them while `reach` holds the furthest end seen so far. A span whose `start` is at or past `reach` shares no block with anything before it, so it opens a new block; either way `reach` grows to cover its `end`.
4. Return `true` when either axis has at least 3 blocks: cut where the second and the third blocks begin.

## Example 1, step by step

- x-axis first: the sorted spans are `[0,2]`, `[0,4]`, `[1,5]`, `[3,5]`. The first opens block 1 and every later one starts before `reach`, so x has a single block.
- y-axis: `[0,2]` opens block 1 and sets `reach = 2`; `[2,4]` starts at `2 >= 2`, opening block 2 with `reach = 4`; `[2,3]` starts inside it; `[4,5]` starts at `4 >= 4`, opening block 3.
- Three blocks on y, so lines at `y = 2` and `y = 4` work and the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m log m) for `m` rectangles: sorting the spans of each axis dominates the linear scan.
- Space: O(m) for the list of spans.

## Pitfalls

- Touching spans are separate blocks: test `start >= reach`, not `start > reach`.
- Keep `reach` as the largest end so far, not the end of the latest span: one long span can cover several short ones that sort after it.
- Check both axes; many grids split only one way.
- `n` plays no part: the rectangles alone decide.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `countBlocks(from, to)` | number of merged blocks on the axis whose coordinates sit at those indices |
| `spans` | each rectangle's `[start, end]` on that axis, sorted by start |
| `blocks` | blocks opened so far |
| `reach` | furthest end among the spans scanned so far |
| `start`, `end` | the span being scanned |

narration.2: countBlocks merges the rectangles' spans on one axis and counts the separate blocks.
narration.3: Project every rectangle onto the axis: rect[from] is where it starts and rect[to] where it ends.
narration.4: Sort the spans by their start so each block is scanned in one piece.
narration.5: No block has been opened yet.
narration.6: reach is the furthest end of any span seen so far.
narration.7: Visit the spans in order of their start.
narration.8: A span starting at or past reach shares no block with the earlier spans, so a line fits right before it.
narration.11: Grow reach to cover this span, keeping the largest end seen.
narration.13: Report how many blocks this axis has.
narration.16: Three or more blocks on the x-axis (vertical lines) or on the y-axis (horizontal lines) make the two cuts possible.
